questions.prompt: Why does prompt specificity (e.g. 'respond with exactly 3 bullet points') tend to produce more reliable results than a vague request?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: A vague prompt leaves the model to guess at format and scope, while a specific prompt directly constrains what a good response looks like

Since the prompt is the model's only interface for understanding the task, being explicit about format and constraints removes ambiguity that would otherwise force the model to guess at your actual intent.
keyPoints: Since the prompt is the model's only interface for understanding the task, being explicit about format and constraints removes ambiguity that would otherwise force the model to guess at your actual intent.

questions.prompt: What is the core idea behind treating generation as 'iterative refinement' rather than a single perfect request?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: Getting an initial output and then giving targeted follow-up feedback to steer it closer to what's wanted, rather than expecting one prompt to be perfect immediately

Iterative refinement treats generation as a short back-and-forth: an initial attempt followed by specific, targeted feedback to steer the output, rather than demanding perfection from a single first prompt.
keyPoints: Iterative refinement treats generation as a short back-and-forth: an initial attempt followed by specific, targeted feedback to steer the output, rather than demanding perfection from a single first prompt.

questions.prompt: Why keep evaluation examples separate from prompt-development examples?
questions.referenceAnswer: Repeatedly tuning against the same examples overfits the prompt to that set. Held-out examples provide a more useful estimate of generalization.
keyPoints: Repeatedly tuning against the same examples overfits the prompt to that set.
Held-out examples provide a more useful estimate of generalization.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between zero-shot and few-shot prompting?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: Zero-shot gives only an instruction with no examples, while few-shot includes a handful of example input-output pairs demonstrating the desired pattern directly in the prompt

Zero-shot relies purely on a described instruction, while few-shot demonstrates the desired input-output pattern with concrete examples embedded in the prompt itself — often a more effective way to specify format and style.
keyPoints: Zero-shot relies purely on a described instruction, while few-shot demonstrates the desired input-output pattern with concrete examples embedded in the prompt itself — often a more effective way to specify format and style.

keyPoints: Since the prompt is the model's only interface for understanding the task, being explicit about format and constraints removes ambiguity that would otherwise force the model to guess at your actual intent.

questions.prompt: Why can the same prompt produce different outputs across separate runs, according to this lesson?
questions.referenceAnswer: The lesson explains that sampling randomness (temperature, top-p, covered earlier in the course) is what causes an unchanged prompt to sometimes yield different outputs across runs.
keyPoints: The lesson explains that sampling randomness (temperature, top-p, covered earlier in the course) is what causes an unchanged prompt to sometimes yield different outputs across runs.

choices.text: Because sampling randomness, like temperature or top-p, introduces run-to-run variation
Because the model's weights change automatically after every single request
Because prompts are randomly rewritten by the system before each run
Because identical prompts are technically impossible to submit twice

questions.prompt: Why is it risky to use too many few-shot examples in a single prompt?
questions.referenceAnswer: Every example adds to the prompt's token count, so stacking too many examples risks hitting context window limits and increasing cost — a direct tradeoff against the benefit each additional example provides.
keyPoints: Every example adds to the prompt's token count, so stacking too many examples risks hitting context window limits and increasing cost — a direct tradeoff against the benefit each additional example provides.

choices.text: There is no downside to including as many examples as possible
Each example consumes tokens, and a prompt with too many examples can run into context length and cost constraints covered in the LLM engineering track
Extra examples always make the model perform worse regardless of context length
Few-shot examples are free and never affect prompt size

questions.prompt: What does framing a prompt with a role or persona (e.g. 'You are a concise technical writer') typically accomplish?
questions.referenceAnswer: A role or persona framing establishes a tone and style expectation up front, similar in spirit to a system prompt's job of setting policy once and having it apply consistently through the rest of the generated content.
keyPoints: A role or persona framing establishes a tone and style expectation up front, similar in spirit to a system prompt's job of setting policy once and having it apply consistently through the rest of the generated content.

choices.text: It has no measurable effect on the response
It sets expectations for tone and style that tend to carry through the response, functioning similarly to a system prompt's policy-setting role
It forces the model to only discuss that specific profession
It guarantees perfect factual accuracy in the response

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson say format control and content control are separate concerns?
questions.referenceAnswer: The lesson explicitly separates these two: controlling structure (format) says nothing about whether the actual claims or information inside are correct.
keyPoints: The lesson explicitly separates these two: controlling structure (format) says nothing about whether the actual claims or information inside are correct.

choices.text: Because instructing how to format a response doesn't guarantee the information within that structure is accurate
Because format and content are always identical properties of a response
Because content correctness is guaranteed the moment format is specified
Because format control is impossible without first controlling content

questions.prompt: Why might a long iterative refinement conversation eventually run into problems?
questions.referenceAnswer: Every turn in a refinement conversation adds tokens to the context, and a sufficiently long conversation can eventually exceed the model's context window, a concern directly tied to the token-budget discussion in the LLM engineering track.
keyPoints: Every turn in a refinement conversation adds tokens to the context, and a sufficiently long conversation can eventually exceed the model's context window, a concern directly tied to the token-budget discussion in the LLM engineering track.

choices.text: Long conversations never cause any technical issues
The accumulated tokens across a long back-and-forth can eventually hit the context window limits covered in the LLM engineering track
Refinement conversations are limited to exactly two turns by design
Only image generation has any limit on conversation length

questions.prompt: What are the key ingredients of an effective system prompt for a production application?
questions.referenceAnswer: A well-constructed system prompt covers purpose, tone, explicit scope boundaries, and a fallback behavior for out-of-scope requests — treating it as a genuine job description for the assistant.
keyPoints: A well-constructed system prompt covers purpose, tone, explicit scope boundaries, and a fallback behavior for out-of-scope requests — treating it as a genuine job description for the assistant.

choices.text: Only a single sentence naming the company
The assistant's role and purpose, tone and style constraints, scope boundaries (what it should and shouldn't do), and how to handle out-of-scope requests
A complete list of every possible user question and its exact answer
System prompts don't need any specific structure at all

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson caution against assuming a system prompt guarantees full compliance?
questions.referenceAnswer: The lesson is explicit that a system prompt is a strong influence, not an unbreakable guarantee — this limitation is covered further in the eval-and-security track.
keyPoints: The lesson is explicit that a system prompt is a strong influence, not an unbreakable guarantee — this limitation is covered further in the eval-and-security track.

choices.text: Because it strongly influences behavior but isn't an unbreakable rule — determined or adversarial users can sometimes get a model to deviate from it
Because system prompts have zero influence on model behavior
Because system prompts are only suggestions with no measurable effect
Because compliance is guaranteed as long as the prompt is under 3 sentences

questions.referenceAnswer: Keep development and held-out evaluation examples separate. Compare versions with the same model settings. Score typical, ambiguous and adversarial inputs against a fixed rubric.
keyPoints: Keep development and held-out evaluation examples separate.

questions.prompt: How would you test that the change fixed this incident rather than hiding it?
questions.referenceAnswer: Keep a reproducible failing case for this incident. Score typical, ambiguous and adversarial inputs against a fixed rubric. Compare the same workload before and after the change; record both the target metric and regressions.
keyPoints: Score typical, ambiguous and adversarial inputs against a fixed rubric.
Compare the same workload before and after the change.
Check regressions as well as the target metric.

questions.prompt: The fix works in a small test but fails at production scale. What next?
questions.referenceAnswer: Keep development and held-out evaluation examples separate. Measure representative workloads and separate resource, data and configuration differences. Stage a rollout with a rollback condition and rerun the original failure case.
keyPoints: Keep development and held-out evaluation examples separate.
Measure a representative workload.
Stage rollout and define rollback criteria.

questions.prompt:
A summarization request needs three factual bullets with source references, but merely asks for a good summary.

What principle should guide the decision in this situation, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer:
A useful prompt specifies the task, audience, required output and success criteria. Separate essential constraints from optional style so evaluation can distinguish correctness from presentation.

Clear output contracts make prompt behavior testable.
keyPoints: Clear output contracts make prompt behavior testable.
A useful prompt specifies the task, audience, required output and success criteria.

questions.prompt:
A support prompt includes five outdated policies alongside the current policy without version labels.

What principle should guide the decision in this situation, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Supply the facts needed for the task with clear source labels and boundaries. Extra context can distract or introduce contradictions; choose information according to the decision being made.

Context should be relevant and unambiguous about source scope.
keyPoints: Context should be relevant and unambiguous about source scope.
Supply the facts needed for the task with clear source labels and boundaries.

questions.prompt:
All classification examples with positive labels mention the same company name.

What principle should guide the decision in this situation, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Examples communicate mappings from inputs to outputs. Cover meaningful variations and edge cases, and avoid examples that contradict the written instruction or contain accidental shortcuts.

Examples should teach the intended rule rather than accidental cues.
keyPoints: Examples should teach the intended rule rather than accidental cues.
Examples communicate mappings from inputs to outputs.

questions.prompt:
An extraction prompt shows only complete invoices and invents values for missing fields.

What principle should guide the decision in this situation, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Ordinary examples show successful behavior; boundary cases show when to abstain, reject or use an unknown value. Include both when the task has ambiguous inputs.

Boundary examples clarify behavior when evidence is incomplete.
keyPoints: Boundary examples clarify behavior when evidence is incomplete.
Ordinary examples show successful behavior; boundary cases show when to abstain, reject or use an unknown value.

questions.prompt:
A valid record contains a correctly typed but unsupported invoice total.

What principle should guide the decision in this situation, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer:
A schema defines fields, types and allowed values. Keep it aligned with downstream needs and use explicit missing-value rules; structural constraints do not guarantee factual correctness.

Structure and factual support require separate validation.
keyPoints: Structure and factual support require separate validation.
A schema defines fields, types and allowed values.

questions.prompt:
A response contains an invalid date even though its JSON syntax is valid.

What principle should guide the decision in this situation, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Parse outputs and enforce required fields, ranges and enumerations in application code. If repair is attempted, bound retries and retain the original failure rather than silently accepting malformed results.

Parsing success does not replace semantic validation.
keyPoints: Parsing success does not replace semantic validation.
Parse outputs and enforce required fields, ranges and enumerations in application code.

questions.prompt:
A summary cites a paragraph that mentions a product but does not support its claimed release date.

What principle should guide the decision in this situation, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Require summaries to preserve source meaning and distinguish claims from interpretation. Citation requirements help auditability only when the cited passage actually supports the statement.

Citations must support the associated claim.
keyPoints: Citations must support the associated claim.
Require summaries to preserve source meaning and distinguish claims from interpretation.

questions.prompt:
An extracted quantity is wrong and then converted correctly into another unit.

What principle should guide the decision in this situation, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Separate evidence extraction from formatting or synthesis when it makes validation easier. Preserve source spans so transformations can be checked against the original, and avoid treating intermediate outputs as infallible.

A correct transformation cannot repair incorrect extracted input.
keyPoints: A correct transformation cannot repair incorrect extracted input.
Separate evidence extraction from formatting or synthesis when it makes validation easier.

questions.prompt:
A prompt is revised repeatedly until it handles five familiar cases but fails on new phrasing.

What principle should guide the decision in this situation, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Collect representative inputs, boundary cases and expected behavior before tuning. Keep a held-out set so prompt edits are not judged only on examples already used for iteration.

Prompt tuning needs unseen evaluation cases.
keyPoints: Prompt tuning needs unseen evaluation cases.
Collect representative inputs, boundary cases and expected behavior before tuning.

questions.prompt:
An answer is well written but omits a required fact.

What principle should guide the decision in this situation, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Use exact parsing, field comparisons or executable checks where appropriate; use a clear human rubric for subjective qualities. Separate correctness, completeness and style instead of blending them into an opaque score.

Evaluation should distinguish factual requirements from style.
keyPoints: Evaluation should distinguish factual requirements from style.
Use exact parsing, field comparisons or executable checks where appropriate; use a clear human rubric for subjective qualities.

questions.prompt:
A retrieved document asks the application to export private notes.

What principle should guide the decision in this situation, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer:
External text may contain instructions that conflict with the task. Preserve source boundaries and enforce access controls outside the prompt; wording alone is not a complete injection defense.

External evidence cannot authorize privileged actions.
keyPoints: External evidence cannot authorize privileged actions.
External text may contain instructions that conflict with the task.

questions.prompt:
A long document leaves insufficient room for the required structured response.

What principle should guide the decision in this situation, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Budget input evidence and expected output together. Remove irrelevant material, preserve mandatory constraints and detect truncation or incomplete results rather than presenting them as finished.

Budget management should preserve essential evidence and completion checks.
keyPoints: Budget management should preserve essential evidence and completion checks.
Budget input evidence and expected output together.
